lessons.title: French Sounds and the Alphabet
lessons.content:
Welcome to your very first French lesson! In the next few minutes, you will go from zero to reading French words aloud with confidence. French has sounds that don't exist in English — but they follow clear, learnable rules.

1. The golden rule: final consonants stay silent

In French, the last letter of a word is usually not pronounced. This single rule will make you sound 50% more French instantly:

WordYou sayNOT
Parispa-REE"Pa-riss"
beaucoup (a lot)bo-KOO"bo-koop"
grand (big)GRAHN"grand"

2. The 5 vowel sounds you must master

French vowelSounds likeExample
a"ah" (like father)la (the)
e"uh" (quick, relaxed)le (the)
i"ee" (like see)merci (thank you)
o"oh" (like go)mot (word)
upurse your lips and say "ee"tu (you)
Pro tip: The French "u" is the sound English speakers fear most. Say "ee", hold it, then round your lips tightly without moving your tongue. That's "tu". Practice 5 times in front of a mirror — it works.

3. Say the alphabet like a French speaker

Repeat each letter aloud: A (ah) · B (bay) · C (say) · D (day) · E (uh) · F (eff) · G (zhay) · H (ahsh) · I (ee) · J (zhee)...

Real-life moment — spelling your name in Lagos

— Votre nom, s'il vous plaît ? (Your name, please?)
— Ade : A — D — E. (ah — day — uh)
— Merci, c'est noté ! (Thank you, got it!)

Your turn (2 minutes): Spell your own first name aloud using the French letter names above. Then spell "NIGERIA": N (enn) — I (ee) — G (zhay) — E (uh) — R (err) — I (ee) — A (ah). Congratulations — you just spoke French.
Today you learned: final consonants are silent · the 5 French vowel sounds · how to say the alphabet and spell your name. In the next lesson: greet anyone, anywhere in the Francophone world.

lessons.title: Greetings and Introductions
lessons.content:
Greetings are the #1 social skill in the Francophone world. In France, Senegal or Côte d'Ivoire, entering a shop without saying "Bonjour" is considered rude — but saying it opens every door. Let's master it.

1. The essential greetings

FrenchWhen to use itMeaning
BonjourMorning until ~6 PMHello / Good day
BonsoirEveningGood evening
SalutFriends, informalHi
Au revoirLeavingGoodbye
À bientôtLeaving, casualSee you soon
Bonne nuitBefore sleeping only!Good night
Warning: "Bonne nuit" is only for bedtime. Leaving a restaurant at 9 PM? Say "Bonsoir" or "Au revoir" — never "Bonne nuit".

2. Introduce yourself in 10 seconds

Three building blocks to memorize:

FrenchMeaning
Je m'appelle Ade.My name is Ade.
Je suis nigérian(e).I am Nigerian.
Enchanté(e) !Nice to meet you!
Real dialogue — two colleagues meeting

— Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Ngozi. Et vous ? (Hello! My name is Ngozi. And you?)
— Je m'appelle Pierre. Enchanté ! (My name is Pierre. Nice to meet you!)
— Enchantée ! (Nice to meet you too!)

Why the extra "e" in "Enchantée"? Women add an "e" (enchantée), men don't. Same sound, different spelling — you can't go wrong when speaking.
Your turn: Stand up and say the full dialogue aloud, playing both roles. Then replace the names with yours: "Bonjour ! Je m'appelle ___. Je suis nigérian(e). Enchanté(e) !"
Today you learned: the 6 essential greetings · when to use bonjour vs bonsoir · how to introduce yourself. Next: count from 1 to 100 and handle prices like a local.

lessons.title: Numbers 1 to 100
lessons.content:
Numbers are everywhere: prices, phone numbers, addresses, dates. Good news — French numbers are logical. Bad news — 70 to 99 have a funny system. We'll make it simple.

1. The foundation: 1 to 20

1 un2 deux3 trois4 quatre5 cinq
6 six7 sept8 huit9 neuf10 dix
11 onze12 douze13 treize14 quatorze15 quinze
16 seize17 dix-sept18 dix-huit19 dix-neuf20 vingt

2. The tens — and the famous French logic

NumberFrenchThe logic
30trente—
40quarante—
50cinquante—
60soixante—
70soixante-dix60 + 10
80quatre-vingts4 × 20
90quatre-vingt-dix4 × 20 + 10
100cent—
Pro tip: 75 = soixante-quinze (60+15). 92 = quatre-vingt-douze (4×20+12). Don't translate — just learn the rhythm: soixante-dix, quatre-vingts, quatre-vingt-dix. It becomes automatic after one week.
Real-life moment — at the market in Abidjan

— C'est combien, les mangues ? (How much are the mangoes?)
— Trois mille cinq cents francs le kilo. (3,500 francs per kilo.)
— OK, j'en prends deux kilos. Voilà sept mille. (OK, I'll take two kilos. Here's 7,000.)

Your turn: Say these prices aloud in French: ₦25,000 (vingt-cinq mille) · ₦75,000 (soixante-quinze mille) · ₦99 (quatre-vingt-dix-neuf). Then say your own phone number, digit by digit.
Today you learned: numbers 1-20 · the tens system · real prices at the market. You've finished the A1 trial! Create your free account to continue with A2 — conversations for daily life.

lessons.title: Talking About Your Day
lessons.content:
"What did you do today?" — this question starts half of all French conversations. To answer it, you need reflexive verbs: the verbs of daily routine. They're easier than they look.

1. The routine verbs (with "se")

FrenchMeaningExample (je form)
se réveillerto wake upje me réveille à 6h
se leverto get upje me lève à 6h30
se laver / se doucherto wash / to showerje me douche vite
s'habillerto get dressedje m'habille
se reposerto restje me repose le soir
se coucherto go to bedje me couche à 23h
The pattern: je me · tu te · il/elle se · nous nous · vous vous · ils se. The little word (me/te/se) is the mirror — the action comes back to you.

2. Build your day, sentence by sentence

Ade's Monday in Lagos

Je me réveille à six heures. (I wake up at 6.)
Je me lève, je me douche et je m'habille. (I get up, shower and get dressed.)
Je prends un café, puis je travaille de neuf heures à cinq heures. (I have a coffee, then I work from 9 to 5.)
Le soir, je me repose avec ma famille. Je me couche vers onze heures. (In the evening I rest with my family. I go to bed around 11.)

Your turn: Write 3 sentences about YOUR morning using: je me réveille à..., je me lève à..., je me douche / je m'habille. Say them aloud twice — speaking is what builds the reflex.
Today you learned: the 6 core reflexive verbs · the me/te/se pattern · how to describe your full day. Next: order food and drinks with total confidence.

lessons.title: At the Restaurant
lessons.content:
Restaurants are where your French becomes real. With 8 phrases, you can handle any table in Paris, Dakar or Douala — from sitting down to paying the bill.

1. The 8 phrases that cover everything

SituationSay thisMeaning
EnteringUne table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.A table for two, please.
OrderingJe voudrais le riz au poulet.I would like the chicken rice.
Ordering (2)Je vais prendre le poisson.I'll have the fish.
DrinksUne bouteille d'eau, s'il vous plaît.A bottle of water, please.
Asking priceC'est combien ?How much is it?
BillL'addition, s'il vous plaît.The bill, please.
PayingJe peux payer par carte ?Can I pay by card?
LeavingC'était très bon, merci !It was very good, thank you!
Golden politeness rule: "Je veux" (I want) sounds demanding in French. Always use "Je voudrais" (I would like) — it's the #1 phrase that makes waiters smile.
Full dialogue — dinner for two

— Bonsoir ! Une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.
— Bien sûr, par ici. Voici le menu. (Of course, this way. Here's the menu.)
— Je voudrais le poulet braisé et une eau minérale. (I'd like the grilled chicken and a mineral water.)
— Très bien. Et pour vous, madame ? (Very good. And for you, madam?)
— Je vais prendre le poisson, merci.
... L'addition, s'il vous plaît. — C'est combien ? — Douze mille francs. — Je peux payer par carte ? — Oui, bien sûr.

Your turn: Play both roles of the dialogue aloud. Then change the dishes: order jollof rice ("le riz jollof") and a juice ("un jus"). In the next lesson: talk about everything you did yesterday.
Today you learned: the 8 restaurant phrases · why "je voudrais" beats "je veux" · a complete dinner dialogue. Next: the passé composé — talking about the past.

lessons.title: Past Events: le passe compose
lessons.content:
"What did you do yesterday?" — after this lesson, you'll answer in full French. The passé composé is the most used past tense in spoken French, and it has a simple recipe.

1. The recipe: helper + past form

The passé composé = avoir or être (present) + past participle:

VerbPast participleExample
visiter (to visit)visitéJ'ai visité Abuja. (I visited Abuja.)
manger (to eat)mangéNous avons mangé du riz. (We ate rice.)
finir (to finish)finiTu as fini le rapport ? (Did you finish the report?)
prendre (to take)prisJ'ai pris un taxi. (I took a taxi.)

2. The être verbs: movement and change

A small family of verbs uses être instead of avoir — mostly movement: aller → je suis allé(e) (I went) · venir → je suis venu(e) (I came) · arriver → je suis arrivé(e) · partir → je suis parti(e).

Memory trick: imagine a house — verbs of coming, going, arriving, leaving use "être". Everything else uses "avoir". That covers 95% of cases.
Real dialogue — Monday morning at the office

— Tu as passé un bon week-end ? (Did you have a good weekend?)
— Oui ! Je suis allé à la plage avec des amis. Et toi ? (Yes! I went to the beach with friends. And you?)
— J'ai visité ma famille à Ibadan. On a mangé ensemble. (I visited my family in Ibadan. We ate together.)

Your turn: Answer in 3 sentences: "Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier ?" Use: j'ai + (mangé / visité / pris / fini) and je suis allé(e) + a place. Say them aloud.
Today you learned: the passé composé recipe · avoir vs être · how to tell your weekend. You've unlocked B1 — where French becomes truly fluent. Create your free account if you haven't yet — the next two lessons are waiting.

lessons.title: Opinions and Connectors
lessons.content:
Welcome to B1 — the level where you stop translating and start thinking in French. The secret? Connectors. They turn short robotic sentences into flowing, natural speech.

1. Give your opinion like a French person

FrenchMeaningRegister
Je pense que...I think that...Everyday
À mon avis,...In my opinion,...Neutral / professional
Je trouve que...I find that...Everyday
Franchement,...Frankly,...Casual
Il me semble que...It seems to me that...Diplomatic

2. Structure your ideas with connectors

GoalConnectors
Order your ideasd'abord (first) · ensuite (then) · enfin (finally)
Add an ideade plus (moreover) · également (also)
Contrasten revanche (on the other hand) · cependant (however)
Concludeen conclusion · c'est pourquoi (that's why)
See the difference — before / after B1

Before (A2): "J'aime Lagos. C'est grand. Il y a du travail. Le trafic est difficile."

After (B1): "À mon avis, Lagos est une ville formidable : d'abord, il y a beaucoup d'opportunités professionnelles ; de plus, l'énergie de la ville est unique. En revanche, le trafic reste un vrai problème."

Exam tip (DELF B1): Using 3 connectors correctly in your speaking test can move you up half a grade. Examiners listen for exactly this.
Your turn: Give YOUR opinion about your city in 3 sentences using: À mon avis... d'abord... en revanche... Say it aloud, slowly, without writing first.
Today you learned: 5 opinion phrases · 8 connectors that structure speech · the before/after B1 transformation. Next: object pronouns — the natives' shortcut.

lessons.title: Object Pronouns: le, la, lui, leur, y, en
lessons.content:
Natives never repeat themselves. "Tu connais Marie ? — Oui, je la connais." That little "la" is an object pronoun — and mastering le / la / lui / leur / y / en is the fastest way to sound natural.

1. The pronouns that replace things and people

PronounReplacesExample
le / la / lesa thing or person (direct)Tu lis le rapport ? — Oui, je le lis. (I'm reading it.)
lui / leur"to" a personJe lui parle demain. (I'm talking to him/her tomorrow.)
yà + place/thingTu vas à Lagos ? — Oui, j'y vais. (I'm going there.)
ende + thing / quantityTu veux du café ? — Oui, j'en veux. (I want some.)
Position rule: the pronoun goes before the verb — the opposite of English. "Je le connais" = I him know. Strange for 3 days, natural after a week.
Real dialogue — at the office

— Tu as vu le nouveau projet ? (Have you seen the new project?)
— Oui, je l'ai vu hier. J'en ai parlé au directeur. (Yes, I saw it yesterday. I talked about it to the director.)
— Et qu'est-ce qu'il en pense ? (And what does he think about it?)
— Il lui faut du temps pour y réfléchir. (He needs time to think about it.)

Your turn: Answer these with a pronoun: 1) Tu aimes le café ? → Oui, je ___ aime. 2) Tu vas au bureau demain ? → Oui, j'___ vais. 3) Tu veux de l'eau ? → Oui, j'___ veux. (Answers: le / y / en)
Today you learned: the 4 object pronouns · the before-the-verb rule · how natives avoid repetition. You've completed the free trial! Ready for the full B1 course? Your journey continues with a subscription.

lessons.title: Professional Email Structure
lessons.content:
French professional emails are more formal than English ones — and more structured. A well-built email earns instant respect from partners in Abidjan, Dakar or Paris. Here is the complete anatomy.

1. The 5 blocks of every professional email

BlockWhat to write
ObjetClear subject: "Demande de devis — commande de juillet"
Formule d'appelMadame, Monsieur, / Bonjour Madame Diallo,
CorpsOne idea per paragraph. Short sentences.
Formule de politesseThe famous long French closing (see below)
SignatureName, title, company, phone

2. Choose your closing formula

FormulaLevel
Cordialement,Standard — 90% of emails
Bien cordialement,Slightly warmer
Dans l'attente de votre retour,When you expect an answer
Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées.Very formal — first contact with an institution
Never do this: starting a first-contact email with "Cher Monsieur" to someone you don't know. The safe, professional standard is "Madame, Monsieur,".
Model email — Lagos exporter writing to an Ivorian partner

Objet : Proposition de partenariat — livraison septembre

Madame, Monsieur,
Je me permets de vous contacter au sujet d'un partenariat commercial entre nos deux sociétés. Nous exportons des produits agricoles depuis Lagos et souhaitons développer notre présence à Abidjan. (I am contacting you about a business partnership. We export agricultural products from Lagos and wish to expand in Abidjan.)
Seriez-vous disponible pour un rendez-vous téléphonique la semaine prochaine ? (Would you be available for a phone call next week?)
Dans l'attente de votre retour, je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, mes salutations distinguées.
Adebayo Okafor — Directeur Commercial, Lagos Agro Export

Your turn: Write a 4-line email to a French supplier: subject, "Madame, Monsieur,", one question about prices ("Pourriez-vous m'envoyer votre liste de prix ?"), and "Cordialement,". Read it aloud.
Today you learned: the 5 email blocks · 4 closing formulas ranked by formality · a complete model email. Next: run a meeting in French — interrupting and agreeing politely.

lessons.title: Meetings: Interrupting and Agreeing Politely
lessons.content:
Meetings are won with formulas, not vocabulary. The French have precise, polite ways to take the floor, disagree and close a point. Master these 15 phrases and you can hold your own in any meeting room.

1. Taking the floor — without being rude

FrenchMeaning
Excusez-moi de vous interrompre, mais...Sorry to interrupt, but...
Si je peux me permettre...If I may...
Je voudrais revenir sur un point.I'd like to come back to a point.
Justement, à ce sujet...Precisely, on that topic...

2. Agreeing and disagreeing like a diplomat

PositionFrench
Full agreementJe suis tout à fait d'accord. · C'est exactement ça.
Partial agreementJe partage votre avis en partie.
Polite disagreementJe comprends votre point de vue, cependant...
Firm but politeJe ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord, et voici pourquoi.
The golden structure: always acknowledge before opposing — "Je comprends votre point de vue, cependant..." Never start with "Non". French professionals hear a direct "non" as aggression.
Real meeting — Lagos regional office

— Pour conclure ce point : nous lancerons le produit en octobre.
— Excusez-moi de vous interrompre, mais je voudrais revenir sur le budget. Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord avec la répartition proposée. (Sorry to interrupt, but I'd like to come back to the budget. I don't fully agree with the proposed split.)
— Je vous écoute. (I'm listening.)
— Je comprends la logique, cependant le marché d'Abidjan demande plus d'investissement marketing. Je propose une révision à la hausse. (I understand the logic, however the Abidjan market needs more marketing investment. I propose an upward revision.)
— C'est un bon point. Nous allons l'étudier. (Good point. We'll look into it.)

Your turn: Imagine a colleague says: "We should reduce the training budget." Respond in 2 sentences: acknowledge + disagree politely, using "Je comprends..., cependant...". Say it aloud three times.
Today you learned: 4 ways to take the floor · the agree/disagree scale · the acknowledge-then-oppose structure. Next: phone calls — the boss level of spoken French.

lessons.title: Phone Calls in French
lessons.content:
No gestures, no lip-reading, no escape — phone calls are the hardest format in any language. The secret: French phone conversations follow a fixed script. Learn the script, and the fear disappears.

1. The phone script, block by block

MomentFrench
AnsweringAllô, Société Camara, bonjour.
Identifying the callerÀ qui ai-je le plaisir ? (Who am I speaking with?)
Asking for someonePourrais-je parler à Madame Diallo, s'il vous plaît ?
Introducing yourselfC'est Adebayo Okafor, de Lagos Agro Export.
Person unavailableElle est en réunion pour le moment.
Hold onNe quittez pas, je vous le passe. (Hold on, I'll put you through.)
MessagePuis-je prendre un message ? / Je lui dirai que vous avez appelé.
Phone survival kit: Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ? (Can you repeat?) · Pouvez-vous épeler ? (Can you spell it?) · Vous pouvez parler plus lentement ? (Can you speak more slowly?). Using these is professional — not a weakness.
Full call — ordering from a supplier in Dakar

— Allô, Sénégal Distribution, bonjour. À qui ai-je le plaisir ?
— Bonjour, c'est Adebayo Okafor, de Lagos Agro Export. Pourrais-je parler à Monsieur Ndiaye ?
— Il est en déplacement aujourd'hui. Puis-je prendre un message ?
— Oui, merci. Pouvez-vous lui demander de me rappeler au sujet du devis ? Mon numéro est le 08 03 22 45 10. (Could you ask him to call me back about the quote?)
— C'est noté. Je répète : zéro-huit, zéro-trois, vingt-deux, quarante-cinq, dix.
— C'est exact. Merci beaucoup, bonne journée !

Numbers by phone: the French say phone numbers in pairs: 06 12 34 56 78 = "zéro-six, douze, trente-quatre, cinquante-six, soixante-dix-huit". Practice saying yours this way.
Your turn: Aloud, play both roles of the dialogue. Then say your own phone number in French, in pairs of digits. Finally, introduce yourself as if calling a new client: "Bonjour, c'est ___, de ___."
Today you learned: the complete phone script · the 3 survival phrases · French phone-number rhythm. Next (premium): presenting a project with confidence.

lessons.title: Essay Structure for DELF B2
lessons.content:
The DELF B2 writing task is not a creativity test — it's an architecture test. Examiners grade your structure before your ideas. Build the right skeleton, and the words will follow.

1. The exam facts

RuleDetail
Length250 words minimum — count them
Time60 minutes: 10 plan · 40 write · 10 proofread
FormatUsually an argumentative essay or formal letter
Graded onStructure · connectors · register · grammar range

2. The winning skeleton: thèse / antithèse / synthèse

PartWhat it doesStart it with
IntroductionHook + question + announce your plan"De nos jours, ..." / "La question mérite d'être posée."
§1 — ThèseArguments FOR one side"D'un côté, il est indéniable que..."
§2 — AntithèseArguments for the other side"En revanche, certains affirment que..."
§3 — SynthèseYOUR position, with nuance"À mon sens, la réalité est plus nuancée..."
ConclusionSummary + opening question"En définitive, ... Reste à savoir si..."
Examiner's secret: a perfectly structured essay with average vocabulary scores higher than a brilliant essay with no structure. Structure first, always.
Skeleton in action — topic: "Le télétravail : progrès ou danger ?"

Intro: "Depuis la pandémie, le télétravail s'est imposé dans nos vies. Mais est-ce un progrès durable ou une menace pour la vie sociale ? Nous examinerons d'abord ses avantages, puis ses limites, avant de proposer une voie équilibrée."
§1: "D'un côté, il est indéniable que le télétravail offre une flexibilité précieuse..."
§2: "En revanche, l'isolement qu'il engendre ne doit pas être sous-estimé..."
§3: "À mon sens, l'avenir appartient aux modèles hybrides..."
Conclusion: "En définitive, le télétravail est un outil : tout dépend de l'usage que nous en faisons. Reste à savoir si les entreprises sauront l'encadrer."

Your turn: Take this topic: "L'anglais doit-il rester obligatoire dans les écoles nigérianes ?" Write ONLY the skeleton: one sentence per part (intro, thèse, antithèse, synthèse, conclusion) using the starters above. 5 sentences = your essay is 50% done.
Today you learned: the exam rules · the 5-part skeleton · ready-to-use starters for each part. Next: formal vs informal — choosing the right register.

lessons.title: Formal vs Informal Register
lessons.content:
The same message can be professional or catastrophic depending on one choice: register. "Salut boss !" in an email to a ministry costs you the contract. Here's how to always pick the right level.

1. The three registers of French

RegisterWhereExample
Soutenu (formal)Administration, exams, first contacts"Je vous saurais gré de bien vouloir..."
Courant (standard)Work, emails, polite conversation"Pourriez-vous m'envoyer le document ?"
Familier (casual)Friends, family, WhatsApp"Tu m'envoies le doc ?"

2. Same word, three levels

Soutenu / courantFamilierEnglish
le travaille boulotwork / job
la voiturela bagnolecar
mangerboufferto eat
dormirpioncerto sleep
l'argentle fricmoney
être fatiguéêtre crevéto be exhausted
Rule of thumb: in writing exams and professional life, use courant — never familier. Understand familier (you'll hear it constantly), but don't produce it until a French friend uses it with you first.
Spot the register — same request, two worlds

WhatsApp to a friend: "Salut Karim ! T'as le temps de relire mon dossier ce week-end ?" (Got time to review my file this weekend?)

Email to a manager: "Bonjour Monsieur Karim, auriez-vous la possibilité de relire mon dossier avant lundi ? Je vous remercie par avance." (Would you be able to review my file before Monday? Thank you in advance.)

Your turn: Upgrade these 3 casual sentences to "courant" register: 1) "C'est crevé, ton boulot ?" 2) "Y'a pas de fric pour le projet." 3) "On bouffe ensemble midi ?" (Possible answers: "Votre travail est épuisant ?" / "Le projet manque de financement." / "Déjeunons-nous ensemble à midi ?")
Today you learned: the 3 registers · 6 word pairs to swap · when to stay "courant". Next (premium): the connectors that make arguments irresistible.

lessons.title: The Francophone World Today
lessons.content:
French is not "the language of France" — it's a world language, and its centre of gravity is moving to Africa. For a Nigerian professional, that shift is a career opportunity, not just a cultural fact.

1. The numbers that matter

FactFigure
French speakers worldwide300+ million
Countries with French as official language29
Francophonie members (OIF)88 states
Biggest francophone countryDR Congo (not France!)
ForecastBy 2050, most French speakers will be African

2. The francophone map, region by region

RegionKey countries
EuropeFrance, Belgique, Suisse, Luxembourg, Monaco
West AfricaSénégal, Côte d'Ivoire, Mali, Burkina Faso, Bénin, Togo, Niger, Guinée
Central AfricaCameroun, RDC, Congo, Gabon, Tchad, Centrafrique
AmericasQuébec (Canada), Haïti
Indian Ocean / AsiaMadagascar, Liban, Vietnam (heritage)
Look at your map: Nigeria is surrounded by francophone countries — Benin, Togo, Niger, Chad, Cameroon. Every cross-border trader, ECOWAS official and international NGO in the region works in both English and French. That's your competitive edge.
Real conversation — why French, why now

— Pourquoi tu apprends le français ? (Why are you learning French?)
— Je travaille avec des clients au Bénin et en Côte d'Ivoire. Sans le français, je perds des contrats. (I work with clients in Benin and Côte d'Ivoire. Without French, I lose contracts.)
— C'est vrai que le français ouvre toute l'Afrique de l'Ouest. (True — French opens all of West Africa.)

Your turn: From memory, name 5 francophone capitals near Nigeria (examples: Porto-Novo, Lomé, Niamey, N'Djamena, Yaoundé, Dakar, Abidjan). Then answer aloud: "Pourquoi le français est-il utile pour moi ?" in 2 sentences.
Today you learned: the real size of the francophone world · why Africa is its future · why Nigeria's location makes French a strategic skill. Next: the social code — tu vs vous.

lessons.title: Social Etiquette: tu vs vous
lessons.content:
Choosing between tu and vous is not grammar — it's diplomacy. Use the wrong one and you sound either arrogant or stiff. The good news: the rules are simpler than people say.

1. The decision table

SituationUse
Stranger, any adultvous
Professional context (client, boss, colleague you don't know well)vous
Older personvous
Friends and familytu
Children and teenagerstu
Online communities, social mediatu (usually)
The escape hatch: when in doubt, start with vous. A French person who wants closeness will offer: "On peut se tutoyer ?" (Shall we use "tu"?). Accept with: "Avec plaisir !" Nobody is ever offended by "vous" — but "tu" too early can sting.

2. Beyond words: the greeting rituals

RitualThe rule
BonjourSay it to EVERYONE — the shopkeeper, the receptionist, the stranger in the lift. Not greeting = rude.
La poignée de main (handshake)Standard in professional and first meetings — light, brief, with eye contact.
La bise (cheek kiss)Friends and family only. NEVER initiate it in business. If offered, follow the other person's lead.
Madame / MonsieurAdd it constantly: "Bonjour Madame", "Merci Monsieur". In France, titles ARE politeness.
Real moment — first day at a francophone partner company

— Bonjour Madame Diallo, enchanté de vous rencontrer. (vous — first contact)
— Enchantée, Monsieur Okafor. Bienvenue à Abidjan !
...two weeks later...
— Dis, Ade, on peut se tutoyer, non ? (Say, Ade, we can use "tu", right?)
— Avec plaisir, Aminata !

Your turn: For each person, choose tu or vous, aloud: 1) your best friend 2) a minister at a conference 3) a 10-year-old child 4) a new client 5) your French friend from university. (Answers: tu, vous, tu, vous, tu.)
Today you learned: the tu/vous decision table · the "On peut se tutoyer ?" ritual · the 4 greeting codes. Next (premium): the history that shaped the Francophone world.

lessons.title: Articles: le, la, les, un, une
lessons.content:
Every French noun has a gender — masculine or feminine — and it never changes. This surprises every English speaker, but French children learn it the same way you will: never learn a noun without its article.

1. The complete article system

Definite ("the")Indefinite ("a/some")
Masculinele — le marché (the market)un — un taxi (a taxi)
Femininela — la banque (the bank)une — une voiture (a car)
Plural (both)les — les enfants (the children)des — des amis (some friends)
Before a vowell' — l'école, l'hôtel—

2. Guess the gender: the ending clues

You can't be 100% sure, but word endings predict gender with impressive accuracy:

Almost always FEMININEAlmost always MASCULINE
-tion / -sion : la nation, la télévision-ment : le gouvernement, le paiement
-té : la liberté, la qualité-age : le fromage, le voyage
-ette / -ie : la baguette, la vie-eau : le bureau, le cadeau
-ure : la voiture, la culture-isme : le tourisme, le journalisme
The habit that changes everything: never write "marché = market" in your notes. Write "le marché = market". The article IS part of the word. Do this from day one and gender stops being a problem forever.
Real-life moment — at a kiosk in Cotonou

— Bonjour ! Vous avez de l'eau fraîche ? (Do you have cold water?)
— Oui. La petite bouteille ou la grande ?
— La grande, s'il vous plaît. Et un paquet de biscuits, et des bananes.
— Voilà. Ça fait mille francs.

Your turn: Guess the article using the ending clues, then say each word aloud: gouvernement (le) · liberté (la) · télévision (la) · voyage (le) · voiture (la) · cadeau (le). Then write 5 words from YOUR daily life with le/la: phone (le téléphone), house (la maison), work (le travail), family (la famille), money (l'argent).
Today you learned: le/la/les + un/une/des · l' before vowels · the 8 ending clues · the golden habit of learning nouns WITH their article. Next: the two most important verbs in French — être and avoir.

lessons.title: Etre and Avoir in Present Tense
lessons.content:
Two verbs carry the entire French language: être (to be) and avoir (to have). Together they appear in almost every sentence you'll ever say — and they're the engine of the past tense. This lesson makes them automatic.

1. ÊTRE — to be

je suis — I amnous sommes — we are
tu es — you arevous êtes — you are (formal/plural)
il/elle est — he/she isils/elles sont — they are

2. AVOIR — to have

j'ai — I havenous avons — we have
tu as — you havevous avez — you have
il/elle a — he/she hasils/elles ont — they have

3. The famous French exceptions: things you "have", not "are"

French logicExampleLiteral meaning
Age uses avoirJ'ai 25 ans."I have 25 years"
Hunger uses avoirJ'ai faim."I have hunger"
Thirst uses avoirNous avons soif."We have thirst"
Fear uses avoirElle a peur."She has fear"
Classic mistake: "Je suis 25 ans" ❌ — always "J'ai 25 ans" ✅. Same for "j'ai faim" (I'm hungry). Remember: age, hunger, thirst, fear are things you carry, not things you are.
Real dialogue — introductions at a workshop in Abuja

— Bonjour ! Je suis Chidi. Je suis ingénieur et j'ai trente-deux ans. (I'm Chidi. I'm an engineer and I'm 32.)
— Enchanté ! Moi, c'est Awa. Nous sommes venus de Dakar pour la formation. (We came from Dakar for the training.)
— Vous avez faim ? La pause déjeuner est à midi. (Are you hungry? Lunch break is at noon.)

Your turn: Complete aloud with être or avoir: 1) Je ___ nigérian. (suis) 2) Tu ___ quel âge ? (as) 3) Nous ___ deux voitures. (avons) 4) Elles ___ fatiguées. (sont) 5) Vous ___ raison. (avez) — then introduce yourself fully: name + profession + age, in French.
Today you learned: full être and avoir conjugations · the "have-not-are" exceptions (age, hunger, fear) · real introductions. You've completed the A1 Foundations course — your base is solid. The A2 course will turn it into conversation.

lessons.title: Making Plans
lessons.content:
Talking about the future in French doesn't require the future tense — 90% of the time, natives use the futur proche: "aller + infinitive". You already know "aller" — you're one step from the future.

1. The formula: ALLER + infinitive

aller (present)+ infinitiveResult
je vaisvisiterJe vais visiter Cotonou. (I'm going to visit Cotonou.)
tu vasmangerTu vas manger quoi ? (What are you going to eat?)
il/elle vapartirElle va partir demain. (She's leaving tomorrow.)
nous allonsregarderNous allons regarder un film. (We're going to watch a film.)
vous allezadorerVous allez adorer ce restaurant. (You're going to love this restaurant.)
ils/elles vontvenirIls vont venir samedi. (They're coming Saturday.)

2. The time words that trigger the future

demain — tomorrowaprès-demain — the day after tomorrow
ce week-end — this weekendla semaine prochaine — next week
le mois prochain — next monthl'année prochaine — next year

3. Invite, accept, decline — the social kit

MoveFrench
InviteÇa te dit d'aller au cinéma ? (Fancy going to the cinema?)
SuggestOn pourrait déjeuner ensemble. (We could have lunch together.)
Check availabilityTu es libre samedi ?
AcceptAvec plaisir ! / Bonne idée !
Decline politelyMalheureusement, je ne peux pas. Une autre fois ?
Real dialogue — planning Saturday in Lagos

— Tu es libre samedi ? Ça te dit d'aller à la plage ?
— Bonne idée ! On part à quelle heure ?
— On va partir vers dix heures. Après, on pourrait manger des fruits de mer. (We'll leave around ten. Afterwards, we could eat seafood.)
— Parfait. Je vais inviter Chidi aussi.
— Génial, on va passer une super journée ! (Great, we're going to have a great day!)

Fluency shortcut: "Ça te dit de... ?" is THE invitation formula among French speakers under 40. Use it and you instantly sound like a native, not a textbook.
Your turn: Plan YOUR next weekend in 3 sentences with "je vais + infinitive": one activity, one place, one person. Example: "Samedi, je vais visiter ma sœur. On va manger ensemble. Dimanche, je vais me reposer." Say it aloud, twice.
Today you learned: the futur proche formula · 6 future time words · the complete invitation kit. You've finished the A2 course — daily conversation is now yours. B1 will make it flow.

lessons.title: Hypotheses: si clauses
lessons.content:
"If I had more time..." — hypotheses are how we dream, negotiate and plan. French "si" clauses follow three strict formulas. Learn the formulas and you'll never hesitate again.

1. The three "si" formulas

TypeFormulaExample
Likelysi + présent → futurSi j'ai le temps, je viendrai. (If I have time, I'll come.)
Unlikely / dreamsi + imparfait → conditionnelSi j'avais le temps, je voyagerais. (If I had time, I would travel.)
Impossible (past regret)si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passéSi j'avais su, je serais venu. (If I had known, I would have come.)
The #1 rule — the "si" trap: NEVER put the future or conditional right after "si". ❌ "Si j'aurai le temps" ✅ "Si j'ai le temps". English speakers make this mistake constantly — examiners and natives hear it instantly.

2. The imparfait you need for formula 2

Take the "nous" form of the present, drop "-ons", add the endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient.

VerbImparfait (je)Example
avoirj'avaisSi j'avais plus de temps...
êtrej'étaisSi j'étais riche...
pouvoirje pouvaisSi je pouvais choisir...
gagnerje gagnaisSi je gagnais à la loterie...
Real conversation — dreams over lunch

— Si tu gagnais un million de dollars, tu ferais quoi ? (If you won a million dollars, what would you do?)
— Si je gagnais un million, j'ouvrirais une école de langues à Lagos. Et toi ? (I would open a language school in Lagos.)
— Moi, si j'avais autant d'argent, je voyagerais dans toute l'Afrique de l'Ouest. (If I had that much money, I would travel all over West Africa.)
— Et si on travaillait dur, on réaliserait peut-être nos rêves ! (And if we worked hard, maybe we'd make our dreams come true!)

Your turn: Complete aloud: 1) Si j'ai le temps ce week-end, je ___ (futur). 2) Si j'avais plus d'argent, je ___ (conditionnel). 3) Si j'étais ministre de l'Éducation, je ___ (conditionnel). Then invent one dream sentence starting with "Si je pouvais...".
Today you learned: the 3 si-formulas · the si-trap (never future after si) · imparfait formation. You've completed the B1 grammar course — your French now handles opinions, shortcuts and dreams. The subscription courses ahead will take you to C1.

lessons.title: Presenting a Project
lessons.content:
A project presentation in French is a performance with a script. Audiences forgive an accent — they never forgive a lost structure. Here is the complete framework used in boardrooms from Paris to Abidjan.

1. The 5-act structure

ActSay this
1. Hook"Bonjour à toutes et à tous, et merci d'être ici."
2. Announce the plan"Aujourd'hui, je vais vous présenter notre projet. Mon exposé comporte trois parties."
3. Navigate"Commençons par le contexte." → "Passons au deuxième point." → "Venons-en à la question du budget."
4. Conclude"Pour conclure, je retiendrai trois messages clés."
5. Questions"Je vous remercie de votre attention. Avez-vous des questions ?"

2. Talk about numbers like an executive

FrenchMeaning
une augmentation de 15 %a 15% increase
nos ventes ont doubléour sales doubled
une baisse significativea significant drop
Comme vous pouvez le voir sur ce graphique...As you can see on this chart...
Les résultats dépassent nos objectifs.The results exceed our targets.
The confidence formula: short sentences + announced structure + steady pace. "Mon exposé comporte trois parties" buys you instant credibility — the audience relaxes because they know where you're going.
Mini-presentation — market expansion project

"Bonjour à toutes et à tous. Aujourd'hui, je vais vous présenter notre projet d'expansion vers le marché ivoirien. Mon exposé comporte trois parties : le contexte, notre stratégie, et les résultats attendus.
Commençons par le contexte. Comme vous pouvez le voir sur ce graphique, la demande a augmenté de 30 % en deux ans.
Passons à notre stratégie : nous ouvrirons un bureau à Abidjan au premier trimestre.
Pour conclure : ce projet dépasse nos objectifs de croissance. Je vous remercie de votre attention — avez-vous des questions ?"

Your turn: Present YOUR real project (or an imaginary one) aloud in exactly 5 sentences: hook, plan announcement, one number, conclusion, question invitation. Time yourself: under 60 seconds. Repeat until smooth — this is your meeting superpower.
Today you learned: the 5-act presentation script · executive number language · a complete mini-presentation model. You've finished the Business course — emails, meetings, calls and presentations are now in your toolkit.

lessons.title: Connectors of Argumentation
lessons.content:
At B2, connectors stop being decoration and become weapons. The difference between a 12/25 and a 20/25 at the DELF is often ten well-chosen connectors. Here is the complete arsenal, ranked by function.

1. The full arsenal by function

FunctionConnectors
Addde plus · en outre · par ailleurs · de surcroît
Explain / causeen effet · car · puisque · dans la mesure où
Opposenéanmoins · toutefois · en revanche · pourtant
Concedecertes... mais · même si · il est vrai que... cependant
Illustratenotamment · ainsi · c'est le cas de · à titre d'exemple
Concludeen définitive · somme toute · par conséquent · c'est pourquoi

2. The royal connector: "bien que" + subjunctive

Bien que (although) demands the subjunctive — and using it correctly is the signature of a B2+ writer:

LevelSentence
B1"Le français est difficile, mais il est utile."
B2+"Bien que le français soit exigeant, il ouvre des portes professionnelles uniques."
Density rule: one connector per sentence maximum, and vary them. Three "cependant" in one essay = lost points. Ten different connectors = the examiner's smile.
Before / after — the same paragraph transformed

Before: "Beaucoup de Nigérians apprennent le français. C'est utile pour les affaires. L'Afrique de l'Ouest est francophone. Il faut des efforts. Le jeu en vaut la chandelle."

After: "De nos jours, de nombreux Nigérians apprennent le français, en effet, la langue est devenue un atout commercial majeur, puisque l'Afrique de l'Ouest est majoritairement francophone. Certes, l'apprentissage exige des efforts ; néanmoins, le jeu en vaut largement la chandelle."

Your turn: Connect these sentence pairs with the right connector: 1) "Le cours est exigeant. ___ il est passionnant." (certes... mais / néanmoins) 2) "Il pleut. ___ le match est annulé." (par conséquent) 3) "L'Afrique compte 29 pays francophones. ___ le Sénégal et la Côte d'Ivoire." (notamment). Then rewrite the "Before" paragraph yourself, differently.
Today you learned: 24 connectors ranked by function · bien que + subjunctive · the density rule. Your writing now argues like a native. Keep practicing with one essay per week — consistency is the final boss.

lessons.title: Key Moments of French History
lessons.content:
You can't fully understand French — its values, its debates, its pride — without the history that forged it. Good news: you only need six moments to follow any cultural conversation.

1. The six moments every francophone knows

YearEventWhy it matters
1789La Révolution françaiseBirth of "Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité" — still the national motto, on every public building
1804Napoléon devient empereurThe Code civil still shapes French law — and legal systems worldwide
1870La Troisième RépubliqueFree, secular, mandatory schooling — France becomes a nation of readers
1944La LibérationEnd of WWII occupation; De Gaulle and national pride rebuilt
1958La Cinquième RépubliqueThe political system France still uses today
1960L'année de l'Afrique17 African nations gain independence — the modern Francophonie is born

2. The vocabulary of French identity

WordMeaning
la RépubliqueNot just a regime — a near-sacred ideal in France
la laïcitéSecularism: strict separation of religion and state, a constant debate
les droits de l'hommeHuman rights — from the 1789 Declaration
la francophonieThe community of French-speaking peoples — YOU are part of it
Conversation key: when a French friend says "C'est la République !" with emotion, they're invoking 1789 — the idea that every citizen is equal before the state. Now you know why.
Discussion point — history and you

1960 connects everything: the independence wave that freed Senegal, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, Togo and Niger is also the reason French remains the language of administration, business and education across West Africa. When you speak French in Lagos, you're using a tool shaped by this exact history — and writing its next chapter.

Your turn: Close your eyes and recite the six dates in order with one keyword each (1789 Révolution · 1804 Napoléon · 1870 République · 1944 Libération · 1958 Cinquième · 1960 Afrique). Then say aloud in French: "Selon moi, l'événement le plus important est ___ parce que ___."
Today you learned: the 6 key moments · the identity vocabulary · how 1960 links France, Africa and your own journey. You've completed the Culture course — félicitations ! You now speak the language AND its story.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Subjunctive
lessons.content:
The subjunctive has a scary reputation — but at B1 you only need it in three situations, with about ten verbs. Natives use it constantly after "il faut que" and "je veux que". Today, it stops being a mystery.

1. When is the subjunctive required?

TriggerExample
Necessity: il faut que...Il faut que tu viennes demain. (You must come tomorrow.)
Wanting: je veux que...Je veux que vous soyez prêts à 9h. (I want you to be ready at 9.)
Emotion / doubt: je suis content que... / je ne pense pas que...Je suis content qu'elle soit là. (I'm glad she's here.)
The mental switch: subjunctive = the action is NOT a fact yet — it's a wish, an obligation, a doubt. If it's a certainty, use the normal indicative. "Je sais qu'il est là" (fact) vs "Je veux qu'il soit là" (wish).

2. The 6 irregular forms you must memorize

Most verbs are regular (remove -ent from "ils" present, add -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent). But these 6 rule the language:

Verbque je...que vous...
êtresoissoyez
avoiraieayez
alleraillealliez
pouvoirpuissepuissiez
fairefassefassiez
savoirsachesachiez
Real dialogue — a manager in Douala

— Il faut que nous finissions le rapport avant vendredi. (We must finish the report before Friday.)
— D'accord. Je veux que tout le monde soit au bureau à huit heures. (I want everyone at the office at eight.)
— Pas de problème. Il faut aussi que je fasse les graphiques ? (Do I also need to make the charts?)
— Oui, et je suis content que tu puisses nous aider sur ça. (Yes, and I'm glad you can help us with that.)

Your turn: Transform aloud into "il faut que...": 1) Tu viens demain. → Il faut que tu ___ (viennes). 2) Vous êtes prêts. → Il faut que vous ___ (soyez). 3) Je fais attention. → Il faut que je ___ (fasse). Then create one real sentence: "Je veux que mon équipe ___".
Today you learned: the 3 trigger situations · the fact-vs-wish switch · the 6 irregular forms. Next (premium): hypotheses with "si" — dreaming and negotiating in French.

questions.text: How do you say "Good morning" in French?
questions.explanation: "Bonjour" is used during the day; "bonsoir" in the evening.

questions.text: Choose the correct article: ___ livre (book, masculine)
questions.explanation: "Livre" is masculine singular, so the definite article is "le".

questions.text: Complete: Je ___ etudiant. (to be)
What is the number "quinze"?
Complete: Comment ___ -vous ? (formal "How are you?")
Which word means "thank you"?
Complete: Nous ___ a Lagos. (habiter)
What does "la semaine" mean?
___ est ton nom ? (What is your name?)
Which is a correct farewell?
questions.explanation: All three are correct ways to say goodbye.

questions.text: Complete: Tu ___ un frere. (avoir)
What is 80 in French?
Choose the feminine form: un etudiant -> ___
Complete: Elles ___ contentes. (etre)
How do you say "my name is Ade"?
What does "s'il vous plait" mean?

Which article before "ecole" (school, starts with a vowel)?
What does "aujourd'hui" mean?
Choose the correct plural: le bureau (desk) -> ___
questions.explanation: Words in -eau take -x in the plural: "les bureaux".

questions.text: Complete (passe compose): Hier, je ___ un email professionnel. (envoyer)
Marie parle a Pierre. Elle ___ parle.
questions.explanation: Indirect object (parler a quelqu'un) uses "lui" for one person.

questions.text: Il faut ___ tu fasses tes devoirs.
questions.explanation: "Il faut que" introduces a clause with the subjunctive.

questions.text: What does "rembourser" mean?
Si j'avais le temps, je ___ plus de francais.
Ce cours est ___ que l'autre. (difficile)
Je cherche la personne ___ m'a envoye ce message.
questions.explanation: "Qui" is the subject of the verb.

questions.text: What does "le chiffre d'affaires" mean?
Avant de partir, ___ tes documents. (imperatif tu)
questions.explanation: Imperative of -er verbs drops the final -s.

questions.text: Which sentence is correct?
options: Je suis alle au marche hier.
Je suis aller au marche hier.
J'ai ete alle au marche hier.

questions.text: Complete: Demain, nous ___ visiter Cotonou. (futur proche)
Every morning, I wake up at 6. = Tous les matins, je ___ a 6h.
Tu veux du cafe ? — Oui, j'___ veux.
At the restaurant, the polite way to order is:
Complete: Elle est ___ a l'heure. (arriver)
What does "l'addition" mean at a restaurant?
questions.explanation: Ask for it with "L'addition, s'il vous plait."

questions.text: Complete: Nous nous ___ tard hier soir. (se coucher)
questions.explanation: Reflexive verbs use "etre" in passe compose: "nous sommes couches".

questions.text: Choose the opposite of "toujours" (always):
Tu vas a Lagos demain ? — Oui, j'___ vais.
Which invitation is correct and natural?
options: Ca te dit d'aller au cinema ?
questions.explanation: "Ca te dit de... ?" is the native invitation formula.

questions.text: Je veux que vous ___ prets a 9h. (etre)
Complete: Tu connais ce film ? — Oui, je ___ ai vu hier.
Si j'avais plus de temps, je ___ apprendre l'espagnol.
Choose the correct connector: "___, il y a beaucoup d'opportunites; ___, le trafic est un probleme."
questions.explanation: "D'un cote... de l'autre" structures a balanced argument.

questions.text: Il faut que je ___ ce rapport avant vendredi. (finir)
Complete: C'est le client ___ je t'ai parle hier.
What is the correct imparfait of "nous finissions"?
questions.explanation: Imparfait describes ongoing or habitual past actions.

questions.text: Complete: Quand j'etais enfant, je ___ au football chaque samedi.
Tu as des nouvelles du projet ? — Oui, j'___ ai parle au directeur.
Which opinion formula is the most professional?
options: A mon avis, cette approche presente des avantages.
questions.explanation: "A mon avis" is the neutral/professional register.

questions.text: Complete: Il est important que nous ___ les resultats demain. (avoir)
What does "en revanche" mean?
questions.explanation: A key contrast connector at B1.

questions.text: Complete: ___ que tu sois, appelle-moi. (Wherever you are)
Choose the correct future: "L'annee prochaine, nous ___ un bureau a Abidjan." (ouvrir)
In a professional email, the standard closing is:
Complete: Bien qu'il ___ tard, il continue a travailler. (etre)
What does "lui" replace in "Je parle a Marie -> Je ___ parle"?
Choose the best sentence for disagreeing politely in a meeting:
options: Je comprends votre point de vue, cependant je vois les choses differemment.

questions.text: Complete: Je ne pense pas que ce ___ une bonne idee. (etre)
questions.explanation: After "je ne pense pas que" (doubt), use the subjunctive.

questions.text: What does "Puis-je prendre un message ?" mean on the phone?
options: Can I speak to the manager?
questions.explanation: A key phrase of the French phone script.

questions.text: Choose the formal register equivalent of "le boulot":
questions.explanation: "Boulot" is familiar; "travail" is the standard/formal term.

questions.text: Complete: ___ le francais soit exigeant, il ouvre des portes uniques.
Which connector introduces an explanation?
Complete: Il se peut qu'ils ___ deja partis. (etre, subjonctif passe)
In the DELF B2 essay, the classic plan is:
questions.explanation: The dialectical plan is the examiners' expected structure.

questions.text: Complete: Les ventes ___ par le nouveau directeur ont double. (present)
What does "par ailleurs" mean?
questions.explanation: "Par ailleurs" adds an argument — a B2 connector.

questions.text: Complete: ___ en travaillant qu'on apprend le mieux. (It is BY working)
questions.explanation: "C'est en + gerondif" = it is by doing.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the gerund correctly?
options: En arrivant, j'ai telephone a Ade.

questions.text: Choose the most formal opening for a first-contact email:
questions.explanation: "Madame, Monsieur," is the safe institutional standard.

questions.text: Complete: Si j'avais su, je ___ venu plus tot.
questions.explanation: Si + plus-que-parfait -> conditionnel passe ("serais venu" — "venir" takes "etre").

questions.text: What is a "nominalisation"? Example:
options: La reduction des couts (instead of "reduire les couts")
questions.explanation: Turning a verb into a noun — the signature of formal French.

questions.text: Which connector concedes before opposing?
Complete: Quoiqu'il ___ , nous livrerons a temps. (arriver)
questions.explanation: "Quoique + subjunctive"; here subjunctive present = indicative form "arrive".

questions.text: The word "soutenu" describes:
Complete: Je doute qu'il ___ la verite. (dire)
What does "en definitive" mean?
questions.explanation: A premium conclusion connector for essays.

questions.text: Choose the B2-level reformulation of "Le projet est difficile mais interessant":
options: Le projet, bien qu'exigeant, presente un reel interet.
Le projet est trop dur, franchement.
questions.explanation: Concession with "bien que" + elevated vocabulary = B2.

questions.text: Complete: Apres ___ termine, il est parti.
In argumentative writing, "notamment" is used to:
Complete: A condition qu'il ___ ses promesses, nous signons. (tenir)
What does the idiom "avoir le cœur sur la main" mean?
questions.explanation: A classic C1 idiom: great generosity.

questions.text: Choose the correct inversion: "___ -on jamais vu pareille croissance ?"
Complete: Il est parti sans que je ___ le temps de reagir. (avoir)
What is "la nominalisation" most typical of?
questions.explanation: "La mise en œuvre de la reforme" instead of "mettre en œuvre".

questions.text: Complete: Quitte a ___ , autant le faire bien. (choisir)
questions.explanation: "Quitte a + infinitive" = if we must / might as well.

questions.text: The expression "mettre les points sur les i" means:
questions.explanation: To be brutally precise — a frequent idiom in debates.

questions.text: Complete: Pour ___ qu'on y reflechisse, la solution n'est pas simple. (autant)
questions.explanation: "Pour peu que + subj." = however much / if even slightly.

questions.text: Which is the correct subjonctif passe of "il finit"?
questions.explanation: Subjonctif passe = subjunctive of auxiliary + participle.

questions.text: "Il n'est question que de..." means:
options: It is only a matter of...

questions.text: Complete: Fussent-ils ___ , ils n'auraient pas signe. (prevenus — even if they had been warned)
What does "un non-dit" refer to?
questions.explanation: Key word of nuanced discourse analysis.

questions.text: Choose the most idiomatic sentence:
questions.explanation: "Il pleut des cordes" = it's raining heavily (idiom).

questions.text: Complete: A supposer qu'il ___ raison, que ferons-nous ?
The verb "se faire" in "il s'est fait voler sa voiture" expresses:
options: a passive with a nuance of misfortune

questions.text: "En un clin d'œil" means:
options: in the blink of an eye / instantly
questions.explanation: Though a wink can also be literal, the idiom = instantly.

questions.text: Complete: Nulle part ___ dans le monde le francais n'est parle autant qu'en Afrique.
questions.explanation: "Nulle part" pairs with "ne" and requires "ou" for place.

questions.text: Which connector best introduces a radical concession?
questions.explanation: "Si... fut-ce" / "fut-ce" = even if it were (literary concession).

questions.text: "Tirer son epingle du jeu" means:
options: to get out of a tricky situation skillfully
questions.explanation: A refined idiom for succeeding against the odds.

questions.text: Complete: Vienne le week-end, nous ___ a la plage. (irons)
questions.explanation: "Vienne le week-end" (subjunctive) = when the weekend comes; main clause in futur simple.

questions.text: Complete: ___ qu'on le veuille ou non, la francophonie evolue.
questions.explanation: "Que... ou non" + subjunctive = whether... or not.

questions.text: The proverb "A beau mentir qui vient de loin" means:
options: it is easy to lie when no one can check your story
questions.explanation: Classic French proverb used in rhetoric.

questions.text: Complete: N'eut ete sa vigilance, l'accident ___ inevitable.
questions.explanation: "N'eut ete" (subj. plus-que-parfait) = had it not been for... + conditionnel passe.

questions.text: What register is "piger" (as in "je piges pas")?
Complete: Il aurait fallu que nous ___ des le debut. (reagir, subj. plus-que-parfait)
questions.explanation: Subjonctif plus-que-parfait: "eussions reagi" — the rarest tense.

questions.text: "Battre son plein" (la fete bat son plein) means:
options: the party is in full swing
questions.explanation: Idiom for an event at its peak.

questions.text: Which sentence shows the gérondif passé?
options: Tout en ayant applaudi, il critiquait la piece.
questions.explanation: "Tout en ayant + participe" = while having done.

questions.text: "Cela ne mange pas de pain" means:
options: it costs nothing to try / why not

questions.text: Complete: ___, j'aurais souhaite etre informe plus tot.
The nuance between "opportun" and "opportuniste":
questions.explanation: C2 is about these fine distinctions.

questions.text: "Renvoyer aux calendes grecques" means:
questions.explanation: Learned idiom: the Greeks had no calends.

questions.text: Complete: Fi des conventions ! Faisons ___ qu'il nous plaise.
Which is the correct "double pronoun" order?
questions.explanation: Order: me/te/nous/vous < le/la/les < lui/leur < y < en.

questions.text: "Etre au taquet" means:
options: to be at full capacity / hyper-focused

questions.text: Complete: Sans compter qu'il ___ encore refuse.
questions.explanation: "Sans compter que" takes the indicative (fact), not subjunctive.

questions.text: "Poser un lapin a quelqu'un" means:
options: to stand someone up (not show up)
questions.explanation: A must-know idiom of everyday French.

questions.text: Which formulation is the most "soutenue"?
options: On a galere grave sur ce projet.
Ce projet nous a mis a rude epreuve.

questions.text: Complete: Quelle que ___ votre decision, je la respecterai. (etre)
"Le torchon brule entre eux" means:
Complete: Je ne connais personne qui ___ autant de langues qu'Ade. (parler)
questions.explanation: Superlative + relative can take the subjunctive ("parle" — same spelling), the C2 subtlety.
